lead: A rectifier is judged by two ratios: how much ripple rides on its average DC, and how much of its AC input current is useful fundamental. The first decides filter size and load heating. The second decides power factor and harmonic pollution. A 50 Hz bridge with a capacitor can draw current in narrow spikes, so its power factor looks poor even when voltage and current cross zero together. This chapter defines the standard numbers — ripple factor, form factor, distortion factor, THD and displacement factor — and shows how they combine into power factor.
prereq: You need: 2.1 for the output waveforms, 2.3 and 2.4 for controlled shapes, and Fourier series basics.

sections.h3: Output quality: average, RMS and ripple

blocks.text: Take the output voltage v_o(t) repeating every T seconds. Its average is the DC value. Its RMS is the heating-equivalent value. The ripple is the AC part left after the average.
V_dc = (1/T)∫₀ᵀ v_o(t) dt,   V_rms = √[(1/T)∫₀ᵀ v_o²(t) dt]
blocks.where: v_o(t) is the output voltage in volts, T is one period in seconds, V_dc is the average output in volts, V_rms is the RMS output in volts.

blocks.text: Ripple factor compares the RMS of the AC ripple to the DC average. The RMS values add in quadrature: V_rms² = V_dc² + V_r,rms².

blocks.where: RF is the ripple factor (dimensionless), V_r,rms is the RMS of the AC ripple in volts, V_dc is the average output in volts, V_rms is the total RMS output in volts.

blocks.text: Form factor FF = V_rms/V_dc = √(1 + RF²). Crest factor CF = V_peak/V_rms. Transformer utilisation factor TUF = P_dc/(V_s,rms I_s,rms), where P_dc is DC power delivered, V_s,rms and I_s,rms are the transformer secondary RMS voltage and current.

Typical values for a resistive load: half-wave RF = 1.21, FF = 1.57; full-wave RF = 0.482, FF = 1.11; three-phase six-pulse RF ≈ 0.042, that is 4.2%. Ripple frequency is f_r = p f_s, where p is the pulse number and f_s is supply frequency. On a 50 Hz supply, a single-phase full bridge has p = 2 and f_r = 100 Hz; a three-phase six-pulse bridge has p = 6 and f_r = 300 Hz.

The supply voltage is nearly sinusoidal, but the input current i_s(t) is not. Write its fundamental RMS as I₁ and its total RMS as I_s,rms. Only the fundamental carries real power with a sine voltage.
PF = P/S = (I₁/I_s,rms) cos φ₁ = DF × cos φ₁
blocks.where: P is real power in watts, S is apparent power in volt-amperes, I₁ is fundamental RMS current in amperes, I_s,rms is total RMS current in amperes, φ₁ is the phase angle between fundamental current and voltage, DF = I₁/I_s,rms is the distortion factor.

blocks.text: The displacement factor is cos φ₁. The distortion factor is DF = I₁/I_s,rms. Therefore PF = DF × displacement factor. A rectifier with perfect phase alignment can still have PF below 1 because of distortion.

blocks.where: THD is total harmonic distortion (dimensionless, often given in %), DF is distortion factor, I₁ and I_s,rms are in amperes.

blocks.text: Some syllabi call THD the harmonic factor; a few write distortion index. Invert the formula when you know THD: DF = 1/√(1 + THD²).

For a single-phase fully controlled bridge in continuous conduction, i_s is a square wave of amplitude I_d delayed by α. Its fundamental peak is 4I_d/π, so I₁ = 2√2 I_d/π = 0.900 I_d. Total RMS is I_d. Thus DF = 2√2/π ≈ 0.900. The fundamental shifts by α, so displacement factor = cos α. PF = (2√2/π) cos α ≈ 0.900 cos α. At α = 0°, PF = 0.900; at α = 90°, PF = 0.

A p-pulse converter has p output pulses per supply cycle. Its characteristic input harmonics are h = kp ± 1, with k = 1, 2, 3, … . A single-phase bridge has p = 2, so h = 1, 3, 5, 7, … — odd only. A three-phase six-pulse bridge has p = 6, so h = 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, … .

A symmetric square current has harmonic amplitude I_h = I₁/h. The third harmonic is 1/3 = 33% of the fundamental, the fifth is 20%, the seventh is 14%, the ninth is 11%. The figure lists these values.

Summing the squares gives THD = √(1/3² + 1/5² + 1/7² + …) = √(π²/8 − 1) ≈ 0.48, about 48% for an ideal square wave. A real bridge with overlap has smaller high-frequency harmonics; see 2.6. Ripple on the DC side repeats p times per cycle, so its lowest harmonic is p f_s. The same p sets both the output ripple frequency and the input harmonic family.

figure.caption: A symmetric square wave contains only odd harmonics, each of amplitude 1/h of the fundamental; the third is 33% and the fifth 20%.

spec.title: Harmonics of a square input current
spec.aria: A table of harmonic orders one, three, five, seven, nine with amplitudes falling as one over h.

examples.question: A single-phase fully controlled bridge supplies a steady load current of 10 A, so the AC input current is a symmetric square wave of peak 10 A. The firing delay is α = 0°. Find the fundamental peak, fundamental RMS, distortion factor, THD and power factor.
steps: Fundamental peak of a square wave of amplitude I = 10 A: I₁p = 4I/π = 4(10)/π = 12.73 A.
Total RMS of a square wave of amplitude 10 A: I_s,rms = 10 A.
Displacement factor = cos α = cos 0° = 1.000. PF = DF × displacement factor = 0.900 × 1.000 = 0.900.
examples.check:
import math
I = 10.0
alpha = 0.0
I1p = round(4*I/math.pi, 2)
I1 = round(I1p/math.sqrt(2), 2)
Irms = I
DF = round(I1/Irms, 3)
THD = round(math.sqrt((1/DF)**2 - 1), 3)
PF = round(DF*math.cos(math.radians(alpha)), 3)
print(I1p)
print(I1)
print(DF)
print(THD)
print(PF)

traps: Displacement factor is not power factor. PF = DF × cos φ₁; a bridge can have cos φ₁ = 1 and PF = 0.90 because of distortion.
A symmetric bridge current has half-wave symmetry, so even harmonics cancel. Listing 2nd, 4th, 6th is wrong.
RF uses the RMS of the ripple, not V_peak − V_dc. Use RF = √[(V_rms/V_dc)² − 1].
THD and DF are linked: DF = 1/√(1 + THD²). Do not subtract THD from 1.
Ripple frequency is p f_s, not f_s. For a single-phase full bridge p = 2, so 100 Hz on a 50 Hz supply.

quiz.q: Define ripple factor and give its formula in terms of V_rms and V_dc.
quiz.a: RF = V_r,rms/V_dc = √[(V_rms/V_dc)² − 1], where V_rms is total output RMS and V_dc is average output.

quiz.q: Which harmonic orders appear in the input current of a symmetric single-phase bridge?
quiz.a: Odd orders only: 1, 3, 5, 7, … . Even harmonics are zero by half-wave symmetry.

quiz.q: Why is power factor written as DF × displacement factor?
quiz.a: PF = P/S = (V_s,rms I₁ cos φ₁)/(V_s,rms I_s,rms) = (I₁/I_s,rms) cos φ₁ = DF × cos φ₁. DF accounts for harmonic current; cos φ₁ accounts for phase shift of the fundamental.

quiz.q: A single-phase fully controlled bridge draws a square current of peak 20 A at α = 60°. Find I₁, DF, THD and PF.
A 50 Hz three-phase six-pulse rectifier feeds a load. Give the lowest input harmonic order and the output ripple frequency.
quiz.a: p = 6, so the lowest characteristic harmonic is h = 5 (then 7). Ripple frequency = p f_s = 6 × 50 = 300 Hz.

quiz.q: At α = 90° the current of a fully controlled bridge is still a square wave. Why is its power factor zero?
quiz.a: The fundamental current is 90° out of phase with the voltage, so cos φ₁ = 0. Real power P = V_s,rms I₁ cos φ₁ = 0. PF = DF × 0 = 0 even though DF = 0.900.

quiz.q: A rectifier has PF = 0.70 and displacement factor = 0.90. Find DF and THD.

beyond: Not for the exam. Grid codes such as IEEE 519 and IEC 61000-3-2 limit harmonic current and set PF targets; real rectifiers add AC chokes, DC chokes, active front ends or PFC stages to meet them. Search terms: characteristic harmonics, total demand distortion, displacement power factor, active rectifier, Vienna rectifier.
